newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN says N.Korea food needs come before politics.
newsitem.headline: UN says N.Korea food needs come before politics.

text.p: Food aid to 800,000 North Korean children should not be held hostage to the politics of the communist state, UNICEF director Carol Bellamy said on Friday.
"People are dying and people are going to die," said Bellamy, who has just returned from North Korea and recently tripled UNICEF aid appeals to $14.3 million.
"It is very important that the immediate significant humanitarian crisis not find itself hostage to what is also a political crisis. Humanitarian needs can't wait," she told a news conference.

The United States, South Korea and Japan, among others, have at one time or another indirectly linked food aid to North Korea's presence at peace talks. North Korea, in turn, has done the same in exchange for its cooperation.

Bellamy, a former New York City Council president and U.S. Peace Corps director, said her U.N. Children's Fund was working closer with the larger World Food Programme operation in North Korea and was concentrating on high-energy milk, medicines and equipment to treat hunger-related diseases.

UNICEF officials said a previous appeal for $3.4 million had been filled with $2.6 million from the European Union and $310,000 from Norway. In addition, Japan's UNICEF committee had raised $300,000 while its counterparts in the United States contributed $60,000. The charity group Oxfam has also sent $82,000 worth of supplies.
In answer to questions, Bellamy said she was in negotiations with both the United States and Japan for funds but was not "as optimistic about Japan as I am with some of the other donors."
Japan, she said, was decreasing its overall foreign aid and was also pulling back from assistance to North Korea.
She said the circle of affected children grew daily, adding: "The results could be catastrophic if these shortages are not eased by winter."
She said about 800,000 children or 38 percent of those under five years of age were suffering from malnutrition.
"We are already seeing children up to the age of 15 who are severely malnourished and in danger of dying," she said. "Starvations hits babies first."
North Korea has suffered from drought this year after food stocks were already depleted by two years of floods.

Bellamy said North Korea was becoming more open to working with humanitarian agencies. But she said long term solutions of agricultural diversification and basic economic organisation were "not being confronted to the extent that they need to be at this point."
